paragraphs.source_en: From the remaining animals represented in the Round Head complex, namely birds, felines, monkeys and insects, only the warthog gives information concerning climate. This animal lives in the moist and arid savanna; it avoids the desert but is able to live in areas without water for several months. When water is available, it drinks regularly and frequents muddy places (Dorst & Dandelot 1983). Images of warthogs are depicted in a few sites in the Tassili. Excavations in the Acacus yielded three remains of warthogs dating between the 9th and the 7th millennium BP, i. e. between the Mesolithic and Pastoral periods (Gautier & Van Neer 1977; Corridi 1998).

paragraphs.source_en: Another category and possible chronological indicator are the (presumed) domesticated animals in the Round Head art. During my fieldwork, among hundreds of wild animal representations in this style, I only found a few possible domesticates. This situation sharply contrasts with the evidence in the Pastoral art where 90% of the animals represented are clearly domesticated cattle. In the Round Head art 90% of animal representations are mouflon and antelope and such a difference in the representation of wild and domesticated animals must be considered fundamental for the two different cultures, namely hunter-gatherers and herders.

paragraphs.source_en: The lack of any other similarities between the Round Head art and the Pastoral images examined during my fieldwork led me to exclude the possibility that the societies producing the Round Head paintings were herders with a productive economy based on domesticated animals. As I will demonstrate throughout this book, the people producing the Round Head images were hunter-gatherers of the Early Holocene who were producing rock art at least 2,000 years before the onset of domestication at around 7,500 years BP (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1999; 2001).

paragraphs.source_en: As for the anthropomorphic figures, they do not seem to give any clear information about the chronology as they are mainly simple static figures, sometimes decorated and masked. Objects associated with them are not chronologically relevant because they are extremely simple forms such as sticks, ovals, possible bags and unrecognisable objects. The only relevant indicator may be the bow, a unique weapon represented in the Round Head art. Muzzolini (1995a: 150) considers this object to be an indicator of a relative chronology within the Saharan rock art. Throughout the Mediterranean the bow was progressively abandoned during more recent millennia, being substituted by the javelin, lance and spear, along with the shield.
